en: A hundred years of human life are like the snap of a finger; before suffering and joy have ended, one suddenly dies.
In the vast and boundless realm of the dead, amidst the chaotic field of consciousness, the solitary spirit is stricken with distress as fame and fortune are all cast away.
It would be better to observe the precepts and recite the Buddha’s name while still alive; among the five precepts, the abstention from killing is foremost.
Among all methods of recollecting the Buddha, holding his name is the easiest. To hold it until the mind becomes one-pointed, the practice accords with the principle.
Observing the precept against killing and holding the name are of equal merit; within this equality, they are distinguished as two matters.
Observing the precept against killing serves as an aid, while holding the name is the primary practice. When merit and wisdom blend harmoniously, the mirror of the mind is clearly revealed.
The Infinite Light of Mindfulness, Boundless Power of Precepts; within the Great Perfect Mirror, the Golden Lotus Blooms.
By the Layman Lianxi of the Hangjiang River.
Table of Contents for the Forty-Eight Dharmas of Reciting the Name.
Guarding the faculty of the mind is called maintaining precepts; guarding the verbal karma is called uprightness of body; holding the beads is called [proper] recitation;
holding with a loud voice is called [proper] recitation; holding with a low voice is called [proper] recitation;
holding like a vajra is called [proper] recitation; holding in silence is called [proper] recitation; regulating the breath is called [proper] recitation; and so forth.
Holding the name according to one's capacity; holding the name wherever one goes, whether in fixed or unfixed locations;
holding the name with a visualized object or without a visualized object; holding the name amidst busyness or in leisure;
holding the name in noble circumstances or in humble circumstances; holding the name in stillness or with subtlety.
Holding the Name with Sincerity; Holding the Name with Joy and Celebration; Holding the Name while Making Vows; Explaining the Meaning of Holding the Name;
Holding the Name with a Sense of Shame and Exertion; Holding the Name with Earnestness; Holding the Name as an Offering;
Holding the Name as a Repayment of Kindness; Holding the Name as an Act of Giving.
Mindfully reciting the name with the mind, listening to the name with the mind; holding the name within sound, holding the name within light, holding the name within a mirror;
holding the name without interruption, holding the name without distraction, holding the name without dwelling;
holding the name is itself Chan and itself Buddha, holding the name is itself precepts and itself Buddha—thus one holds the name.
Holding the name while teaching; holding the name without holding it; holding it while not holding it; holding the name alone;
holding the name by setting a time limit; holding the name in assembly;
holding the name until accomplishment; holding the name for others; holding the name in times of difficulty; and holding the name in dreams.
Holding the Name During Illness, Holding the Name at the Hour of Death, Making Vows, Repentance, and Holding the Name:
The Forty-Eight Methods of Holding the Name (with Preface).
Composed by Zheng Weian of Jiangdu.

If we discuss the Pure Land, its dharma-gates are vast and expansive. Those superior and virtuous people who, relying on the Buddha’s teachings, have attained rebirth there arrive from the ten directions in numbers as numerous as raindrops.
Among them, some did not focus exclusively on mindfulness of the Buddha during their practice, nor did they focus exclusively on the recitation of the Name during their mindfulness;
yet they have already loftily inscribed their names and titles and sit securely upon the golden terraces. This is likely because they...

Great vows, or perhaps through sublime awakening, or by possessing manifold merits, or by upholding the power of the precepts, or through diligent visualization—thus, without relying on external expedients, one spontaneously attains the opening of the mind.
Speaking of the present day, visualization is not easily accomplished; the precepts are not easily maintained in their entirety;
manifold merits cannot be expected in a morning or an evening; and sublime awakening is not attainable for those of dull faculties.
One’s great vows are firm and steadfast; indeed, such are rarely found.

If one does not emerge from the practice of sincerely holding the Name and attain a state of transcendence, one will inevitably sink long into the sea of suffering and undergo saṃsāra forever. Even the compassion of a thousand Buddhas would find it difficult to save you.
Therefore, this single method of holding the Name universally accommodates those of the three capacities, leading them swiftly back to the Pure Land. There is no superior expedient means than this.
Beyond this, whether one’s practice is deep or shallow, harmonious or fragmented, depends entirely on what one takes up for oneself. Strive in your future path; do not allow yourself to err.

Regarding the guarding of the faculty of mind (*manendriya*), since you have already begun to recite the name with this mind, you need not concern yourself with any other miscellaneous good or evil matters whatsoever.
On that very day, attend to necessary circumstances. If there are duties that cannot be avoided, complete them and then let them go;

do not allow them to entangle you so as to obstruct the movement of your mind. Furthermore, the reason my thoughts become entangled is because the mental ground (*manobhūmi*) is occupied with affairs.
If your mindfulness reaches the luminosity of the mind-ground (*cittabhūmi*), the mental ground will naturally excel at observation. You should know this regarding mindfulness.
The Buddha can transform the ordinary into the sagely; it is the foremost method for liberation within both the mundane and supramundane realms.
Since one recites the name while maintaining the precepts of verbal karma, all acts of killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and falsehood must not be uttered from the mouth.
Do not toy with your head. If you become involved in such things, you should reflect for yourself: "A person who recites the Buddha's name ought not to act like this.
Then, forcefully recite the Buddha's name several times to remind yourself and cleanse your mind.
Regarding "upright body and holding the name":
since one recollects the Buddha with this very body, one must strive to remain constantly upright during all activities—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down.
If the body is upright, the mind will immediately become pure; you should test this for yourself, for it truly does not deceive us.
Passing the beads while reciting the name of the Buddha once for each bead, recite the four characters alone. Do not intermingle them with the six characters;
it is easier to achieve a continuous flow of mindfulness with the four characters. Within these four characters, one may pass the beads over the character "A" (阿) or over the character "Da" (陀).
Passing the beads, one must establish a fixed scope and not allow them to become disordered; this is a method for using the beads to bind the mind.
When the spirit and intellect are dull or when delusive thoughts arise in profusion, rouse the spirit and recite the name aloud.

When the Buddha reaches several hundred recitations, one naturally undergoes a transformation of one's state of awareness. Furthermore, the faculty of hearing is most acute and is easily influenced by external conditions;
when sounds trigger the mind, various discursive thoughts flare up intensely. Only by chanting the Buddha’s name aloud can one protect the faculty of hearing.
Thus, the spirit-mind is awakened. The mind listens to its own sound; with every sound, there is complete fulfillment. All notions of right and wrong naturally cease and are dispelled.
Recite the name in a low voice.
If the spirit is scattered or when one is oppressed by extreme exhaustion, there is no need for a loud voice;
simply gather the faculties and recite with a low, subtle voice. Wait until the breath is stabilized and the spirit is revitalized, and then you may recite the Buddha’s name aloud.
Regarding the Vajradhara recitation:

if the mind or breath is uncomfortable, or if there are obstacles from people or the environment, such that loud or low voices are all found inconvenient, then one should simply move the lips while employing the Vajradhara method.
There is no restriction on the number of repetitions; however, each and every syllable must arise from the mind.
If one passes the beads too quickly,
it is unsuitable whether one silently holds the name or recites it in a loud or low voice. Furthermore, passing the beads with the hand is considered tedious and trivial by the Vajra [Master].
Maintain this, yet still feel dissatisfied with the lingering traces [of effort]. There is an ancient, supremely skillful expedient that requires no movement of the mouth and produces no sound;
it merely requires fixing the mind on a single object and slightly striking the front teeth with the tongue-root. As the mind’s attention responds accordingly, the sound becomes distinct.

The sound does not transcend the orifice, yet the faculty of hearing is internally integrated. The mind seals the mechanism of the tongue, and as the mechanism is drawn forth, the root of discursive thought is uprooted.
Entering the stream through hearing, one turns the hearing back toward one's own nature; these three are unified, becoming perfectly penetrating in every thought-moment.
After a long time, this eventually becomes the contemplation of mind-only consciousness.
Regarding the regulation of breath while holding the name:
when the breath is calm and the mind is tranquil, first visualize your own body within a circle of light. Silently contemplate the tip of the nose and observe the inhalation and exhalation.
With each breath, silently recite the name of Amitābha Buddha once. This is the expedient means for regulating the breath.

Neither lax nor hurried, let the mind and breath rely upon one another, following their movement in and out. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, practice this at all times without interruption.
Constantly maintain it in secret. Once the gathering of the mind has continued for a long time, both breath and thought will be forgotten.
This very body and mind will then become equal to empty space. When mastery is attained through such sustained practice, the eye of the mind opens and the samādhi suddenly manifests.
This is precisely the Pure Land of Mind-Only.

If, while reciting the name according to one's capacity, drowsiness frequently occurs, then one should maintain the practice by walking meditation (*caṅkrama*). If at times distraction and confusion are frequent, then one should sit upright.

One should maintain it. Even if one's walking or sitting is not appropriate, whether kneeling, standing, or even briefly reclining, one should extensively employ skillful means to maintain the Name, saving oneself according to one's capacity; this is essential regarding the four characters of the Great Name.
To be unwilling to forget for even a single thought-moment is the essential art for subduing the demons of the mind. Wherever one is—
whether in a pure or impure place, in leisure or in busyness, in moments of joy or in times of despondency— one should simply turn [the mind] back and recite the name.

The light turned back to reflect upon itself, and he thought to himself: "As for these various realms, I have experienced hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, and billions of them since time immemorial.
Yet, regarding the single matter of rebirth through mindfulness of the Buddha, I have been unable to bring it to completion.
For this reason, I have wandered through the cycle of saṃsāra, unable to emerge from it. Now, I shall no longer concern myself with whether I can recite [the Buddha's name] or not."
If you cannot maintain mindfulness, simply vow with this mind of mindfulness of the Buddha: "Until death, I shall never sever this thought. Why is this?
Because if the thought of mindfulness of the Buddha is severed, all manner of miscellaneous thoughts—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral—will arise once again.
Even when one is at the point of passing stool or urine, or when a woman is giving birth, one should continue to focus solely on mindfulness. Beyond this...

One must transcend both suffering and mindfulness. One must transcend pain and mindfulness, just as a child calls out to its mother; one need not concern oneself with whether the mother finds it distasteful or not.
If I were afraid of her disapproval and failed to call out, then for the child who has fallen into a pit or a latrine, there would be nothing but death—on what day could he ever see his mother again?
Regarding "having fixed times": this refers to establishing fixed periods for practice.
During the two sessions of morning and evening, one sets a regular schedule that shall remain constant from now until death, neither increasing nor decreasing.
During the remaining twelve periods of the day, if one can recite even a single phrase—reciting that single phrase regardless of whether it is in a loud or low voice—it is as the ancients said:
"Speak fewer words; recite more phrases of the Buddha. How true! How true indeed!
When holding the name while facing the image, one takes this very image as the true Buddha, not restricted to a single direction and regardless of the three bodies (trikāya). One simply contemplates:
"I rest my mind on one; the mind rests on one Buddha. Facing the Buddha with mental recitation, one’s sincerity and reverence will be evident. Sincerity and reverence.
Upon reaching this state, one must certainly invoke spiritual inspiration. If no Buddha image is present, one should sit upright facing the west.

Whenever thoughts arise or the mind moves, one should visualize the radiance of Amitābha Buddha abiding upon the crown of one’s head. With every word and every phrase, [one should maintain this visualization].
If one does not fall into emptiness, even black karma can be extinguished.
If one can hold the Name amidst the bustle—
even if it be but one phrase, or ten phrases— so long as one attains even a fragment [of mindfulness] amidst the midst of great turmoil, [the karmic obstacles will be eliminated].
In the intervals between carving, you may set aside your body and mind and chant with clarity. As the poem by Bai Juyi says:
"Walking, it is Amitābha; sitting, it is Amitābha. Even if one is as busy as a speeding arrow, one does not depart from Amitābha."
The application of mind by the ancients can thus be seen.

Among those who hold to names in their leisure, all are people of the world suffering from various afflictions; they seek leisure but cannot find it, and therefore are unable to practice. Now that you have leisure, yet again—
Upon hearing this method of *nien-fo*, you must ensure that your practice is continuous and seamless; only by exerting yourself with focused composure can you avoid wasting your time.
If you allow your mindfulness to drift away in negligence, it will fail to accomplish anything, merely protracting the years in vain and betraying the four debts of gratitude.
When the Old Lord Yama comes to summon you one day, with what will you offer in response?

The fortune of being noble and holding [the Buddha’s] name in this life has been cultivated through previous existences. Those of noble station are for the most part the reincarnations of eminent monks who practiced austerities.
Yet, despite such glory, it cannot endure; should one further create evil karma, one will surely sink into the depths of suffering.
You should reflect for yourself: rather than returning home burdened by karmic obstacles, it would be better to "row the boat with the current.

Whether by establishing a hall for reciting the Buddha's name, selecting monks who practice mindfulness of the Buddha, carving scriptures on the Pure Land, or enshrining images of Amitābha, you may ascend a high place and call out;

thus, with half the effort, you shall achieve double the result. Furthermore, you should resolutely vow to be reborn there, regardless of whether you are wealthy or poor, noble or lowly. All should do so.
A model for human practice, a messenger of the Dharma King—how exalted you are!
Alas, how base and lowly it is to merely hold the name.
To serve as a slave to others is suffering; not to seek liberation from it is the suffering of sufferings. One should know these four.

Recite the Buddha’s name. Regardless of whether one is noble or humble, high-born or lowly, old or young, male or female, if one can, every morning at dawn, with a sincere heart, face west and recite His name ten times, seeking rebirth in Ultimate Bliss without interruption or cessation, one will obtain benefit in the present life and attain rebirth in the Pure Land after death.
Amitābha Buddha truly saves those drowning in the sea of suffering.
It is like a boat.

Since you have already attained wisdom by holding the name with tranquility and subtlety, do not allow it to enter into madness. It is most appropriate to recite the Buddha’s name with tranquility and subtlety, thereby making it firm and stable. You should...
If those who possess wisdom and insight practice the recollection of the Buddha (buddhānusmṛti), then those among the world who practice the recollection of the Buddha will surely become numerous.
If those with wisdom and insight practice the recollection of the Buddha, then practitioners of external paths (tīrthika) will easily turn back [from their ways]. Why is this?
It is because they are inspired by the reputation of one possessing wisdom and rescued by the transformative power of one possessing wisdom.
To sincerely hold the Name, seeking neither fame nor profit and not displaying one's talents, and to practice with such sincerity—this is most difficult to find. As the Patriarch said:
"In the midst of Zen practice, one cannot find a single person who is dull-witted enough [to succeed]. Those who recite the Buddha’s name today are precisely...
I fear only that people may not be free from delusion and dullness. The two characters "old" and "sincere" (lǎo-shí) constitute the direct, straight path for birth in the Western Land.
Why is this so? To be "old and sincere" means not to add even a hair’s breadth of discursive thought beyond the four characters of Amitābha Buddha.
Rejoicing in the holding of the Name may arise from people or from events; even the most minor instances are all joyful states of human life.
One should know that such joy is illusory and cannot endure forever. Seizing this favorable moment, turn the light inward and recite [the Name].
If one relies upon the Buddha’s radiance, then within favorable circumstances, one will eliminate many evil thoughts;
auspiciousness will continue in succession, and one will practice according to one's wishes until the end of life, attaining rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss—is this not truly a great joy?
Holding the name through the making of vows is originally for the purpose of rebirth in the Pure Land. However, the majestic radiance of the Buddhas is inconceivable;

by reciting their names, one’s aspirations will be fulfilled according to the heart’s desire. Therefore, the sutras state that there are ten kinds of benefits from mindfulness of the Buddha. Rather than [seeking] prayers...

To pray to ghosts and spirits, to perform miscellaneous ritual repentances, to extensively indulge in evil vows, and to peripherally rely on shamans and sorcerers—these are not as effective as taking the recitation of the Buddha's name as one’s goal.

Someone might say: "What if they do not respond? I answer: "If you have not yet recited the Buddha's name, yet first worry that there will be no response, this very cause of non-response will inevitably bring about the fruit of non-response. Such is the cause; such is [the result]."
The Fruit. How terrifying!

A Commentary on the Ten Benefits of Reciting the Buddha’s Name: (1) One constantly obtains the protection of great powerful celestial generals who remain invisible throughout the day and night; (2) One constantly encounters the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.

1. He shall be protected by all the Bodhisattvas and the three Amitābha Buddhas, who will constantly emit light to gather this person under their care. 2. All evil spirits and all venomous snakes or poisonous drugs shall be unable to cause harm. 3.

All great calamities involving water, fire, or weapons, as well as untimely deaths, unjust deaths, imprisonment, and the like, shall not befall them. 4. All previously committed sins shall be completely extinguished; there shall be no further pursuit by those whose lives they have taken. 5.

In dreams at night, they shall experience upright visions or see the body of the Buddha. 6. Their minds shall always be joyful, and whatever they do shall be auspicious and successful. 7. They shall always be honored and provided with offerings by all the people of the world. 8. At the time of death, their minds shall be free from fear and remain correct.
When mindfulness manifests, one personally sees the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas emitting light to welcome and lead one to rebirth in the Western Land).
This explains that when any adverse conditions arise before one, they are all encounters with past karmic conditions; one must not give rise to further evil thoughts.
As for the unfinished karmic causes that will arise in the future, you need only accept them as they come. Where they can be avoided, avoid them; where they can be neutralized, neutralize them.

Simply follow the conditions of cause and effect, and do not forget to recite the Buddha’s name. Since the Buddha possesses immeasurable wisdom and merit, when his light shines upon you, adverse circumstances and conditions will immediately transform; of this there is no doubt.

Feeling shame and exerting oneself to uphold one's reputation—whether in this life or in previous existences—the fruition of evil is already established, and the retribution of suffering will inevitably arrive.

Thus, every portion of suffering corresponds to a portion of evil. One must not excuse this by claiming that fortune and destiny are unevenly distributed; rather, one should simply feel shame for one’s own failure in practice.

It is not too early. Every time one contemplates the Buddha, the hairs on the body stand on end and the five viscera feel as if they will tear apart; one is moved by such sorrow and agitation that one feels pained and does not wish to live.
When it is thus, every word flows forth from the very marrow of one's bones; only then is this the true realm of mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*).
Among the monastics and laypeople who practice mindfulness of the Buddha today, some recite with their mouths while their minds wander elsewhere, while others focus their minds when they recite.

When one rests, the mind becomes dull. Furthermore, when reciting the Buddha's name, if one intersperses it with miscellaneous speech, then even if one continues this practice until the end of one’s life, no spiritual response will ever arise.
When others see this, they will conclude that the teachings on rebirth through the recitation of the Buddha’s name are ultimately empty words.
How could this be the fault of the Buddha?
To earnestly hold the Name while encountering circumstances beyond one's power and yet not feel sorrow is contrary to human feeling.
However, to encounter circumstances beyond one's power and merely wallow in grief—how could such a person be said to understand Buddha-nature? Since...
How tragic! One should therefore contemplate escaping from suffering; one should contemplate bringing all sentient beings ultimately out of suffering;
and one should contemplate why the Buddha is called "Greatly Compassionate"—it is because He is able to pull sentient beings out of suffering.
As I recollect the Buddha with a heart of compassion, seeking the Buddha’s compassion to pull me from my own suffering, how should this recollection be earnest?
Furthermore, when making offerings to those who uphold the Name,
whenever one encounters auspicious festivals or the Buddha’s birthday, one should offer incense, flowers, lamps, and fruit according to one's means; this is called material offering.
Offerings. These are offerings that are not in accordance with the Dharma. Offerings made with the mind surpass all material offerings. Lately, heterodox teachings have flourished;
they extensively gather sacrificial items for superior offerings—what benefit does this bring to spiritual cultivation? It is like [the principles of] Pure Conduct and Universal Salvation.

The Huangji (Imperial Ultimate), Shouyuan (Source of Longevity), Wuweizong (School of Non-action), Dacheng (Mahāyāna), and various other heterodox teachings summon souls and attract ghosts, depleting people's wealth and indulging in arrogant falsehoods;
yet they stand in stark contrast to the single gate of Buddha-recitation. Those with discernment [should recognize this].
Do not be deluded by this at all.
To repay the kindness of the Heaven, Earth, the Sovereign, and one’s parents through the practice of holding the Name is the greatest of all kindnesses. How should one repay it? First.
To provide all manner of food and drink as offerings, to establish merit and spread one's fame—judged by the standards of worldly dharma, such retribution is certainly not unwholesome.
Yet, this is ultimately not the final resolution. I simply repay them by reciting the Buddha’s name and dedicating it toward the Western Paradise;
thus, I have already planted a seed of Vajra. When they emerge again, there will naturally be a time for their liberation, let alone those who are infinite in number.
Can all karmic obstacles be completely dissolved? Those who wish to repay the Buddha’s kindness must not fail to know this Dharma.

When practicing giving or reciting the Name, whenever one encounters those in distress, one should first bring peace to their body, and only then guide their mind by exhorting them to recite the Buddha's name.
To save from suffering for a single lifetime, giving is urgent; to save from suffering throughout kalpas, reciting the Buddha’s name is essential.
If one sees people or beings in distress and lacks the power to rescue them, one should immediately recite the Buddha’s name on their behalf to settle their spirit and consciousness.
Or, one may chant clearly at the quiet night to bestow merit upon ghosts and spirits. In years of great military conflict or widespread epidemics, [the practice of] the five...
Furthermore, by reciting the Buddha’s name, one can eliminate resentment and pestilence.

One should contemplate that this single utterance of "Amitābha Buddha" reaches upward to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and downward to the Wind-Circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*); all sentient beings throughout the dust-like lands receive benefit simultaneously.
Its merit of giving is inconceivable.
One contemplates with the mind, listens with the mind, and upholds the name with the mind;
only after this does one move the tongue. When the tongue moves, it returns once more to the mind. Once the tongue has produced sound, the ear listens to itself.
This is what is meant by "contemplating with the mind and listening with the mind. When one contemplates with the mind and listens with the mind, the eyes are naturally unable [to see].
The eyes cannot falsely look; the nose cannot falsely smell; the body cannot falsely move.
This one true master has been invited forth by the four characters of Amitābha Buddha.
Once the sound of holding the name while reciting the Buddha’s name has become thoroughly proficient, among the six sense objects there is only the single object of sound.
The functions of all six sense organs are entirely entrusted to the ear; the body is not even aware of its circumambulation, nor is the tongue aware of its movement.
It moves. The mind does not perceive its own discrimination; the nose does not perceive its own inhalation and exhalation; the eyes do not perceive their own opening and closing.
The two perfect penetrations of Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta are one and the same. There is nothing that is not permeated, and there is nothing that is not perfect.
The sense organ (*indriya*) is the sense object (*viṣaya*); the sense object is the sense organ. The sense organ and the sense object are consciousness (*vijñāna*).
The eighteen realms (aṣṭādaśa-dhātu) are thus fused into a single realm. At first, one may not yet be disciplined; after a long time, one will naturally enter [this state].
Whenever reciting the Buddha’s name, take a clean area of four or five feet and circumambulate it once to the right. Then, slowly produce a sound, gradually raising its volume.
Recite in this manner until, after three circumambulations, you perceive that the sound of your own mind has been revealed. Continue to rotate...
It encircles space, encompassing the ten directions and pervading the entire Dharma-realm;
this is the dwelling of body and mind within the sound of Buddha-recitation. Thus, with this very body and mind, one dwells within the sound of Buddha-recitation while reciting the Buddha's name.
This is a supreme state that can extinguish the defilements of the mind; one should diligently practice it.
Those who hold the name within the light do so through the voice of the mind; the light is likewise the light of the mind.
Wherever the voice of the mind circulates, there the light of the mind shines forth. To practice *buddhānusmṛti* while abiding within the voice of the mind is to abide within the light.
To recite the Buddha’s name while clearly visualizing [the image] within the mirror is likewise a sublime state that can extinguish the defilements of the mind; one should diligently practice this.

As the sound of the voice holding the name revolves within the mirror, the light of the mind radiates forth, and the essence of the mind naturally reveals itself. Indeed, this is the One True [Reality].
The mind is like a great, perfectly round mirror, penetrating all things without obstruction.

The Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time, sentient beings, the wheel of suffering in the turbid world, and the lotus calyxes in the pure lands—all are but reflections within this mirror. Sound is identical to light, and light is identical to the mirror.
This is the most supreme realm, capable of forever extinguishing the defilements of the mind; one should apply oneself with diligence to its practice.
One should continuously maintain the recitation of the name:
reciting it in the morning, reciting it in the evening, reciting it when there is nothing to do, reciting it when there is something to do, and reciting it in clean places as well as in defiled ones.
In every state of mind, there is not a single thought that is not the Buddha.

Even when one is engaged in the daily affairs of responding to others and there are moments of interruption, though those verbal expressions may cease, their true life-vein cannot be severed. When one’s practice reaches this point, it will be easy for it to become a continuous, unified mass.

"Holding the name without admixture": "without admixture" refers to *śamatha* (calm abiding). *Śamatha* is the vehicle for *samādhi* (concentration). By ceasing discursive thoughts, right mindfulness manifests.
There are three types of discursive thoughts: first, wholesome thoughts; second, unwholesome thoughts; and third, neutral thoughts. These three are to be eliminated.
[The Master] said, "It is a settled principle that those who cherish life attain longevity, while those who indulge in killing meet an early death.
Yet, how can it be that some who cherish life die young, while others who indulge in killing live long?"
The answer is: Retribution is of three kinds. First, that which is performed in this life and the retribution for which is received in this life.

Second, that which is received in a future life. Third, that which is received over many lives and many kalpas. To be born well but die prematurely is the result of evil karma from past lives; not being born well is likewise so.
"Then their lifespan will become even shorter. That one who loves killing yet lives long is due to the merit of past lives; had they not loved killing, they would not have lived this long.

The guest said, "I, so-and-so, have also observed the precept against killing and practiced the release of living beings, as well as reciting sutras and mantras, yet I do not see any reward for it now."
Why is this? The answer is: the slowness or swiftness of retribution depends solely on whether the conditions (*pratyaya*) have ripened or not.

To seek swift retribution when the conditions have not yet arrived is like hoping for a harvest immediately after having just sown the seed. Furthermore, to avoid unexpected calamities is itself a blessing; how could it be otherwise?
"Do you not know that there is one who silently bestows protection?
The guest asked, "One comes to know fear and dread only when retribution is manifested in the present. When it is delayed until a future life, everyone considers it remote and vague.
Why does Heaven not cause people to receive their retribution immediately?"

The answer is: The speed with which retribution is received depends merely on the sequence of causes and conditions; it is not due to Heaven. To insist that one must wait for a manifest reward in this life before believing is the height of folly.

(In the tenth year of the Xianfeng era, I was lodging with Xu Yuyi of Lusi. There was a beggar there who had lost a leg. He said to people: "In years past, I left some meat on the ground and it was eaten by a dog.

I cut off its leg with a knife, whereupon the dog carried the leg to the Land Temple and died while howling. A month later, I developed a carbuncle from which the bone emerged. All the local people know of this. Is this not a manifest retribution from Heaven?"—Lianxi.)
[Postscript by the Layman].
A guest asked: "Why is it that when a certain person has not yet cultivated merit, their wishes are fulfilled, but after performing virtuous deeds, they encounter misfortune at every turn?"

The answer is: This is indeed due to past karma that was destined to receive a heavy retribution; however, because he performed good deeds, the heavy [retribution] has been transformed into a light one.

It is like a prisoner condemned to death who, when the winter execution order is about to be carried out, encounters a great amnesty before the appointed time arrives, whereby his sentence is changed to flogging and he is released.
The guest said: "A person who kills living beings causes other species to be unable to protect their offspring; such a person ought to receive the retribution of having no heirs.
Yet, among those whose karmic burden of killing is heaviest—such as fishermen—why is it that their progeny are particularly numerous?"
The answer is: Among the children of the world, there are those brought about by merit and those brought about by misdeeds.
For instance, due to the karmic power of a fisherman, he may have a wicked family who divide his food and clothing, causing him to toil day and night without having enough for their shared use;
the more children he has, the heavier his burden becomes. Do you not see that the celestial immortals and the lunar mansions never give birth?
The guest said, "When one is born into this world, one ought to study the sages and worthies and learn the way to serve the sovereign and benefit the people.
What does the doctrine of cause and effect have to do with the state of the world and the hearts of men?"

The response states: The doctrine of cause and effect is precisely the Way of the sages and worthies. Sentient beings of the final age indulge in evil deeds, neither fearing the laws of the state nor regarding integrity and shame;
yet when they reflect upon them alone in the quiet of night, they still dare not openly commit evil, fearing only the retribution they will receive after death.
Thus, the Buddhist teaching of cause and effect truly serves as a supplement to the teachings of the sages.
This is the royal framework [of the teaching].
[The fourth question] concerns the doubt as to whether evil karma exists or not.
The guest said: "Humans are the most intelligent among all things, yet they may even mistake enmity for gratitude; animals are at the height of stupidity, yet they..."
One can repay enmity and requite kindness.
Why is this? The answer is: regarding the repayment of favors and the settling of grudges, there are cases that are conceivable and those that are inconceivable.

The retribution for the karma of killing may be delayed or immediate; once the karmic adversary arrives, no one—whether a celestial being, a seer, a human, or a ghost—can escape it. [This applies even to] animals.
He was born; it was simply that he could not speak, which was particularly distressing. His grievances and favors were indeed perfectly clear and distinct.
The guest said, "The doctrine of hell is merely intended to exhort people toward goodness; how could it truly exist?"
The respondent said: "Since there are prisons in the human world, how could they alone be absent from the netherworld? The Buddha does not utter deceptive words to mislead people.
The guest said: "I see that hell exists right here in the world of the living; those such as beggars with empty bellies are [the denizens of hell]."
Hungry ghosts are those whose bodies are bound by shackles and fetters; this is itself hell. The Sword-Tree and Knife-Mountain are precisely the moments when animals are being slaughtered.
The boiling cauldrons and glowing coals are precisely the times when animals are being seared and stewed.
The answer is: This statement may seem plausible, but in reality it is not so.

It might be acceptable to say that there are hells within the world of the living, but it is unacceptable to say that hell is actually located within the world of the living. For example, a foolish person may be compared to an animal;
does this mean that, apart from such people, there are no other animals with fur and horns?
The guest said, "Hell certainly exists, but it is recorded only in non-Confucian texts (*wàishū*). A Confucian scholar ought not to speak of it.

I replied, "If one wishes to avoid mentioning it with one's mouth, it is better to first avoid it with one's person. If one has found the way to avoid it, then even when encountering others who urge one to discuss it, it is permissible [to remain silent].
Otherwise, one must simply refrain from speaking of it altogether. If hell truly exists, would there be no Confucian scholars within it?"
Resolving Doubts Regarding the Observance of the Fast and the Abstinence from Meat (The Seventh Question).
A guest asked: "To kill or injure living beings is certainly a great sin; as for eating meat, one might suppose there is no fault.
Yet the sutras state that eating meat inevitably results in retribution for evil deeds. How stringent is the law of the unseen realm!"
The answer is: It is not only in the world beyond; the laws of this world are likewise. Killing is comparable to robbery, and eating meat is comparable to harboring a robber.
How far apart can the one who harbors the thief and the thief himself be? People simply have not reflected upon this.
The guest said, "Food and clothing are all determined by prior karma; when one's merit is great, what one enjoys is likewise abundant.
As for those who observe the fast, 'binding a vow with the mouth' refers to binding oneself to a seven-day period. If one binds such a vow alone, one may use dried provisions."
Fruits and sweets, ginger, and sesame oil—these four constitute the food.

Incense ashes, lamp oil, a meditation cushion, a chair, a cotton robe, a wind-hat, a cleansing bucket, and toilet paper—these eight are the necessary utensils. Apart from these twelve items, one should leave nothing else behind.
Thus, for seven days, one may remain without socializing with others and recite the Buddha’s name with ease. If...

There were five or six people who, having collectively resolved their intention, agreed upon a fixed period; they necessarily invited a master to serve as the guardian of the seven-day retreat, strictly established rules and regulations, and placed these constraints at the forefront.
For the duration of the seven days, all activities—including rising and resting, eating and drinking, and the offering of incense and flowers—were governed by these precepts.
The fruit of the lamp is to protect the seven masters; when illumination and response are fully complete, one is identical to those seven.

Thus, for seven days, one may also recollect the Buddha with a sincere mind. However, those who are bound by emotional views and do not understand the benefits and harms of spiritual practice should not undertake this rashly.
When four or five people gather spontaneously to hold a *nienfo* assembly, they must first establish their rules before opening their mouths to recite the four characters.
Recite one character for each stroke of the incense burner; use a small hand-chime (*qing*), striking it specifically on the character "Tuo" (陀), and do not [strike it] otherwise.
Irregular and disordered, it instead leads to a distracted mind.

One might instead assist others in upholding the Name, or have them settled in a quiet place; or one might join them in a vow of recitation, or inform them of the matters concerning the Pure Land, or borrow...
By means of the scriptures on the Pure Land, one may either dispel doubts regarding the practice of *nienfo* or strengthen the resolve for *nienfo*.
Among all merits, this is the most supreme. Furthermore, if one recites the Buddha’s name for another at the moment of their death, [the merit is even greater].
Alternatively, one may have the patient memorize the four characters of Amitābha Buddha’s name;

by recollecting and mindfulness of them as they arise, the person shall behold the Tathāgata and, upon the exhaustion of their breath, attain rebirth. This is the fulfillment of their dharmakāya and the life-force of wisdom.
Holding the Name Amidst Difficulties:
Whenever there is one who resolves to practice mindfulness of the Buddha amidst difficulties, there will surely be a miraculous response.

Even if the land is filled with the clash of weapons or a region is afflicted by pestilence, those who seek the Buddha’s protection will find peace for every single person and peace for every hundred people. This is not due to anyone other than the Buddha.
Even in the presence of private attachments, one responds within the light of equality without deliberate thought. Why is this?

If, upon stirring a thought or uttering a sound, one perceives that Amitābha Buddha’s radiance rests upon the crown of one's head, then naturally, every moment will be complete, every moment firm, and every moment enduring.
Under the influence of the Buddha’s light and the protection of auspicious deities, one will spontaneously [attain these qualities].
Avoid obstacles; do not let your thoughts wander.

If the power of your vow in holding the name is firm during dreams and your practice is matured—being continuous and dense by day and likewise at night—then you will naturally be able to [do so] within dreams.
Recite the Buddha’s name; this is the omen of rebirth in the Pure Land. You should harmonize your practice with diligent effort, neither falling into despondency nor succumbing to agitation.

For a patient who maintains the Name during illness, it is the very moment of death. Death is the threshold between the ordinary and the sage, and between the pure and the defiled. During illness, you must act accordingly.
Contemplate death and diligently recite the Buddha’s name, resolving that you will certainly await death;

then there will surely be light to welcome and guide you, thereby fulfilling your vow for rebirth in the Pure Land. If, however, during an illness you fixate on the boundaries of this world, then all forms of attachment, fear, afflictions, anxieties, and various distracting thoughts will arise simultaneously.
At such a critical juncture of life and death, how can you possibly manage the matter?
Formerly, there was a monk who fell gravely ill. He would involuntarily cry out "A-ye. Realizing this was improper, he immediately began to recite the name of Amitābha Buddha.
Although his pain did not cease, with every cry of "A-ye" he would respond with a single recitation of "Amitābha Buddha," continuing without interruption day and night.
When his illness finally healed, he said to others: "During my illness, I recited 'A-ye' and I recited the name of Amitābha Buddha. Now that my illness..."
"Very well. Amitābha Buddha still remains, yet Emperor Wu has acted wrongly.
One does not know that there will surely come a day when one must relinquish this body. Those who slander the Buddha-dharma relinquish their bodies in hell;
those who are greedy for wealth and beauty relinquish their bodies as hungry ghosts; those who are deluded..."

As for sensual desires, they lead one to cast away one's body among the animals. One fears that seeking [liberation] through the "casting away of the body" (sheshen) like Emperor Wu of Liang at Tongtai Temple will not be possible.
As for the loss of the empire, it was precisely because he could cast away his body but could not cast away his mind.
Had he been able to cast away his mind and transcend the world, he would have regarded the empire as worn-out sandals; how could he have reached such a state in his declining years?
If he invited Hou Jing with the intent of seizing the Central Plains, one can see that his three days of "giving up the body" did not exempt him from the thought of seeking blessings;
it was simply that he could not bear to abandon the empire. How could he have truly abandoned the entire world?
The guest said: "Since we Confucians recite and follow the teachings of Confucius, it is our duty to repel heterodox doctrines.
Why do you, sir, instead support those on the left?"
The answer is: Generally speaking, what the world calls "heterodox" (yìduān) refers to that which differs from the great principles of the Sage.

For instance, compassion (*cèyǐn*) is the principle of benevolence (*rén*); to lack it is heterodoxy. A sense of shame and aversion (*xiū'è*) is the principle of righteousness (*yì*); to lack it is heterodoxy.
The Sage is free from fixed intentions, compulsions, stubbornness, and self-centeredness; to possess these is heterodoxy. The Five Precepts of the Buddha are... [text continues]

These are the Five Constant Virtues. Nowadays, when those who slander the Buddha hear that the doctrine of compassion originates from the Buddha, they invariably reject that doctrine, whereby our own benevolence (*ren*) is lost.
When they hear that the prohibitions against theft and sexual misconduct originate from the Buddha, they invariably reject those prohibitions, whereby our own righteousness (*yi*) perishes.
When they hear that the prohibition against false speech originates from the Buddha, they invariably reject it...
Because of their precepts, our people’s faith has consequently been extinguished; is this not a case of seeking to protect the Way while, on the contrary, harming it?
Moreover, the Way of the Sages is one of great public-mindedness and selflessness. From Yao and Shun down to Confucius, we hear of no mutual attacks or refutations.
It was only when Mencius opposed Yang Zhu and Mo Di that he did so—opposing their "selfishness" which harms benevolence (*ren*), and their "universal love" which harms righteousness (*yi*).
This is righteousness (*yi*). The Buddha’s pursuit of the mutual benefit of self and others is precisely what is called the simultaneous fulfillment of benevolence (*ren*) and righteousness (*yi*).
How could it be compared to that of Yang Zhu or Mo Di? Later generations failed to discern this, conflating Buddhism with the teachings of Yang and Mo and treating them as one;
thus they rejected it, their indignant fury growing ever more intense. From this day forward, there is no knowing where it will end. It is for this reason that I [write this].
I am fearful; therefore, I have spoken of this matter. Whether you recognize me or blame me, what further calculation could there be? Appendix: Mr.
Zheng Weian’s Verses on Prohibiting Killing and Releasing Living Beings (Seven Poems), Set to the Tune of "West River Moon" (*Xījiāngyuè*).
Heaven favors life and abhors killing. Humans ought to refrain from killing and practice the release of living beings. Do not, for the sake of food, set knife and block to work.

Exhausting one's entire lifetime of merit, the fish, shrimp, turtles, and tortoises of the watery realms, and the beasts and birds that roam the forests—all share this same spiritual mind with humans.
To take life is inevitably to invite the demand for one’s own life in return.
One life must be repaid with one life; a thousand blades shall be requited with a thousand blades. How could a thousand lifetimes or a hundred kalpas ever extinguish this?
Amidst the swirling chaos of kalpas, one creates it for oneself—there is no need to seek divinations or consult the lot. Know that when one is under the sway of a kalpa, it is impossible to escape.
If you seek clemency from the Celestial Bureau, the merit of abstaining from killing is most sublime.
To kill another in a past life was myself; to be killed by another in this life is myself. Thus, through such topsy-turvy confusion, one becomes an enemy to oneself.
When will I finally be able to let go? It would be better for me to first abstain from killing. Once a virtuous mind is stirred, it is boundless;
auspicious deities will protect one like clouds and mists, sparing the four elements from injury and mutilation.

When will this quest for vengeance come to an end? Through the reversal of causes and conditions, they become enemies. I urge people to rest early while there is still time; by repenting, one can yet save oneself.
I preach releasing living beings and reciting the Buddha’s name; it is like a boat upon the bitter sea.
One who is able to diligently practice this Dharma can resolve the entanglements of resentment and be free from blame.
In the past, there was a man surnamed Shen whose family had for generations specialized in bestowing kindness upon aquatic creatures. Having gathered treasures in a pond, he obtained a golden basin.
Gold and silver appear inexhaustibly through transformation; a single sparrow brought a ring to repay its debt of gratitude. The Yang family enlarged their gate because of this.
All living beings possess vital energy and a spiritual root; do not harm these humble creatures.

There was also the True Man Simiao, who released fish and saved a divine dragon; his medicinal prescriptions were passed down, widely manifesting merit, as he attained entry into the ranks of the immortals among phoenixes and cranes.
Most excellent was the elderly monk of the Lotus Pond, whose writings on releasing life and abstaining from killing were so skillful.
Mind after mind, one dedicates merit to reach the Lotus Palace;

those of the highest grade attain rebirth with honor, wealth, and nobility in the divine realms of the Buddha-lands—all of which arise from the practice of abstaining from killing. Why, then, should we harbor further doubts?
Bitterly burdened by boundless karmic debts, the clash of arms rages everywhere. Alas for those who flee east and west!
Each person should quickly extinguish their murderous intent to ensure the safety and peace of their own home and family.
